stem: Your CI job runs an Agent SDK harness that reviews the pull request, and the harness stops after 3 iterations because the team wanted reviews to stay quick. Last month 31% of jobs ended while the final response still carried stop_reason "tool_use", and those jobs posted a review that had never read the changed test files. What is the correct control flow?

options.text: Raise the iteration cap from 3 to 25, which covers the observed distribution of tool calls per review.
Post the partial review with a banner saying the job hit its limit, and let the reviewer rerun the job.
Continue while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stop on "end_turn", keeping the cap as a runaway guard.
Move the review to a model with a larger context window so the whole diff is read without repeated tool calls.

explanation: stop_reason is the loop's control signal. An iteration cap is a safety net against a runaway loop, not the mechanism that decides the review is finished.

why.A: A larger number is still an arbitrary stopping decision, so the same truncation returns on any longer review.
why.B: Shifts detection of an incomplete review onto the reviewer instead of fixing the loop.
why.D: Context size does not change the fact that the model asked for another tool call and was cut off.

stem: Your codebase exploration harness wraps every tool execution in a try/except. When Grep exits non-zero because a path no longer exists, the harness catches the exception, breaks out of the loop and returns the last assistant text. 18% of sessions end this way with a half-written answer. What is the right change?

options.text: Retry the failing tool three times with a growing delay, and break out of the loop only if all three attempts fail.
Append the failure as that call's tool_result and keep looping, so the model can choose another path or tool.
Validate every path with Glob before the harness issues a Grep call, so calls that would fail are never made.
Return the exception text to the engineer and let them restart the session with a corrected prompt.

explanation: A failed tool call is information the model should receive. Returning it as the tool result keeps termination under stop_reason control and lets the model adapt.

why.A: Retries do not help when the path is simply gone, and the loop still ends on an error the model never saw.
why.C: Pre-validating one tool's arguments cannot cover the other failure modes, and it moves decisions out of the loop.
why.D: Turns a recoverable tool error into manual work for the engineer.

stem: A helper script your team uses for multi-file refactors sends an extra message after every assistant turn asking "Is the task complete? Reply COMPLETE or CONTINUE." This doubles the number of requests, and on 7% of runs the model replies COMPLETE while files it had listed as pending are still unedited. What should the script do instead?

options.text: Keep the completion question but require the model to list the files still pending, and continue while that list is non-empty.
Ask for the completion answer inside a JSON object so the script can parse the reply without ambiguity.
Drop the question and stop as soon as the assistant turn contains a text block, since a finished refactor ends with a summary.
Read stop_reason on each response, executing tools while it is "tool_use" and finishing on "end_turn".

explanation: The API already reports whether the model wants another tool call. A self-reported completion check is an extra round trip and a probabilistic signal.

why.A: Still asks the model to judge its own completion, which is the signal that is already wrong on 7% of runs.
why.B: Parsing is not the problem; a well formed COMPLETE is still an opinion rather than a control signal.
why.C: A single turn can carry text and tool_use blocks together, so text presence is not a completion indicator.

stem: Your CI coordinator delegates a pull request to four review subagents in parallel. When the tests subagent exceeds its time limit its Task call returns an error, and the coordinator logs that error and goes on to synthesis with the three results it does have. The posted review reads as complete. Three pull requests merged last month with no test comment and a suite that was already failing. What is the correct coordinator change?

options.text: Handle the failed delegation at the coordinator: re-delegate it, and hold the review back if that still returns nothing.
Have the tests subagent catch its own timeout and return whatever partial findings it has, so synthesis always receives four inputs.
Raise the tests subagent time limit to the point where the timeout stops occurring on pull requests of this size.
Have the synthesis subagent count the result sets it received and note in the posted review when one of the four is missing.

explanation: The coordinator owns delegation, so a delegation that failed is its error to resolve. Continuing to synthesis with a silent gap turns a recoverable failure into a review that looks finished.

why.B: A partial result from a timed-out agent is indistinguishable from a complete one, and it moves error handling out of the hub.
why.C: Addresses one cause of one failure; any other subagent error still passes through the same silent path.
why.D: Puts detection in a subagent that was working correctly, and an annotated review still ships with the gap unfilled.

stem: You ask your Claude Code coordinator to audit the payments module for dead code. The exploration subagent reports accurately on the files it was given, the analysis subagent's findings check out, and the report is coherent. It lists 30 unused HTTP handlers and nothing else, although the module also holds queue consumers, cron entry points and a webhook dispatcher. The coordinator log shows three subtasks: "unused route handlers", "unused request validators", "unused response serializers". What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: The exploration subagent's Glob patterns matched only files under the http directory, so nothing else was ever read.
The report step dropped the non-HTTP findings because its template has one section per route handler.
The coordinator decomposed the audit into three HTTP-shaped subtasks, so the other entry points were never assigned.
The analysis subagent used a dead-code definition that requires an unreferenced route, excluding queue and cron code.

explanation: The coordinator's own log shows a decomposition that covers only the HTTP surface. Each subagent executed its assignment correctly, and the assignment is where the gap is.

why.A: Blames a subagent that reported accurately on the subtasks it was handed.
why.B: Nothing suggests findings were produced and then dropped; they were never requested.
why.D: The analysis subagent's findings check out for the subtasks it received.

stem: Your three search subagents each append their results to one shared findings file that the synthesis subagent later reads. On last night's run two of them wrote within the same second and one agent's 14 sources vanished from the final report, while the coordinator log shows all three returning success. Which change fits the hub-and-spoke design?

options.text: Add a file lock so each subagent waits its turn before appending its findings to the shared file.
Run the three search subagents sequentially, so only one of them is ever writing to the file.
Give each subagent its own findings file and have the synthesis subagent read all three of them at the start of its pass.
Have each subagent return findings to the coordinator, which aggregates them and passes the set to synthesis.

explanation: Aggregating subagent results is the coordinator's job. Routing findings back through it removes the shared mutable state and gives the coordinator a view of what each subagent actually produced.

why.A: A lock stops the overwrite but leaves aggregation happening in a file the coordinator never sees.
why.B: Pays the latency of three sequential searches and still depends on shared mutable state.
why.C: Removes the collision but keeps information flowing around the coordinator, which still cannot tell that an agent returned nothing.

stem: Your CI coordinator delegates a 22-file pull request to three review subagents, each told "review this pull request". Reviewers report that about 40% of the posted comments are near-duplicates across the three, and the two migration files in the change received no comments at all. Which two coordinator changes address this? (Select 2)

options.text: Assign each subagent a distinct slice of the change, by file group or by concern, so the assignments do not overlap.
Have the coordinator drop any posted comment whose text closely matches one already posted by another subagent.
Check the set of assignments against the list of changed files before delegating, so nothing is left unassigned.
Let the subagents exchange their in-progress comment lists so each can skip what another has already covered.

explanation: Both symptoms come from the coordinator's assignment step: overlapping briefs produce duplicate comments, and an incomplete brief leaves files uncovered.

why.B: Deduplication after the fact hides the overlap and does nothing for the two unreviewed migration files.
why.D: Peer-to-peer coordination removes the coordinator's view of who covered what and still guarantees nothing about coverage.

stem: Your coordinator builds each review subagent prompt by concatenating a 400-word block of team review conventions with the file under review. The block is pasted at three call sites in the coordinator script. A teammate updated one of the three, and for two weeks the security subagent applied a rule the other two subagents did not, so the same pull request drew contradictory comments. Where do the conventions belong?

options.text: In the coordinator system prompt, so one copy governs every review it delegates.
In a conventions file that each subagent is instructed to read before it starts reviewing its file.
In the Task prompts still, but generated from one shared constant so all three call sites emit identical text.
In the review subagent AgentDefinition system prompt, leaving each Task prompt to carry only the file under review.

explanation: Conventions are standing behavior that never varies between invocations, which is what the AgentDefinition system prompt is for. The per-call prompt should carry only what changes from call to call.

why.A: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator context, so conventions in its system prompt never reach the agent writing the comments.
why.B: Costs a tool call per invocation and depends on the subagent choosing to read the file before it starts.
why.C: Removes this instance of the drift and still resends 400 words on every call, with the conventions living in the caller rather than in the agent.

stem: Your coordinator invokes the same review subagent once per file, 30 times for a large pull request. On file 3 the subagent read the shared auth helper and described its contract correctly. On file 19 it re-derives that contract from scratch, reaches a different conclusion, and the two comments contradict each other. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Turn on memory sharing between invocations of the same subagent type so later calls can see what earlier ones read.
Include the auth helper's contract, established in a first pass, in each per-file invocation's prompt.
Review all 30 files in a single subagent invocation so the helper is read once and stays in context.
Have the subagent append its conclusions to a scratch file and instruct it to read that file before each review.

explanation: Separate subagent invocations share no memory, so any fact that must hold across all of them belongs in the prompt the coordinator hands each one.

why.A: Subagent invocations do not share memory, and there is no setting that makes them.
why.C: Trades the contradiction for attention dilution across 30 files in one pass.
why.D: Depends on the subagent choosing to read the file and on whatever earlier passes happened to write, when the coordinator already holds the fact.

stem: The AgentDefinition for your document analysis subagent lists allowedTools as ["Read", "Grep", "Task"]. Traces from one research run show that subagent spawning four subagents of its own, while the coordinator log records a single delegation and the run cost six times the estimate. What should change?

options.text: Keep Task on the analysis subagent but cap how many subagents any one agent may spawn within a run.
Leave the tool list alone and have the coordinator sum the usage of nested agents so the cost is at least visible.
Remove Task from the analysis subagent's allowedTools so only the coordinator can spawn subagents.
Describe the nested work as steps in the coordinator's system prompt so it performs that analysis in one place.

explanation: Task belongs to the coordinator alone. Leaving it in a subagent's allowedTools lets delegation happen outside the hub, which is why one delegation appears in the log and five agents appear on the bill.

why.A: A cap limits the blast radius but keeps delegation happening where the coordinator cannot see it.
why.B: Reporting cost afterwards does not restore the coordinator's control over which agents run.
why.D: Rewrites a prompt without removing the tool that let the subagent delegate.

stem: Two of your subagents carry the AgentDefinition descriptions "Analyzes code" and "Reviews code". Engineers report that codebase orientation questions go to the review subagent about half the time, and its answers are shallow because its system prompt is written for defect hunting. Both subagents perform well when invoked deliberately, and two more code subagents are planned this quarter. What is the most effective first step?

options.text: Rewrite both descriptions to state what each one handles, typical requests, and when to prefer it over the other.
Merge the two into one code_agent whose system prompt decides internally whether to orient or to hunt for defects.
Add a coordinator instruction sending orientation questions to the analysis subagent and defect hunts to the review one.
Strengthen the review subagent's system prompt so its answers to orientation questions come out more thorough.

explanation: The description is what the coordinator selects on, and two vague near-identical descriptions give it nothing to discriminate with. Rewriting them is the smallest change that addresses the misrouting.

why.B: A consolidation may be defensible later, but it rebuilds both agents when neither description yet says what it covers.
why.C: Moves routing rules into the coordinator prompt, which then needs an edit for every subagent added.
why.D: Improves an agent that was invoked for the wrong kind of question; selection is what is failing.

stem: Your pipeline agent can call run_tests and post_verdict, and policy is that no approve verdict may be posted unless the suite has run and passed. An audit of 4,100 pull requests found that 9% of approvals were posted without run_tests ever being called, mostly on changes the agent judged too small to need tests. What change enforces the policy?

options.text: Add a system prompt rule stating that run_tests must be called before any approve verdict, with no exceptions.
Block post_verdict with an approve value until run_tests has returned a passing result in the same run.
Add few-shot examples showing small changes that still require a test run before the approval is posted.
Run a nightly job that re-runs the suite for merged pull requests and opens an issue whenever a test fails.

explanation: Approve-without-tests is an ordering requirement with a real consequence, so it needs a programmatic prerequisite rather than an instruction the model may set aside.

why.A: Instructions have a non-zero failure rate, which is exactly what the 9% figure measures.
why.C: Examples shift likelihood and cannot guarantee the call happens on the next unusual diff.
why.D: Detects the problem after the code merged instead of preventing the unverified approval.

stem: Your agent escalates mid-conversation while the customer is still in the chat. The handoff payload carries the customer ID, a root cause summary and a recommended action. Human agents report that in one handoff in six they re-issue a refund the agent had already processed, or contradict something the agent had promised. Which two items should the handoff add? (Select 2)

options.text: The agent's confidence in its own root cause analysis, so the human knows how far to trust the summary.
The actions already executed in this conversation with their identifiers, such as the refund reference.
The full turn-by-turn transcript, so the human can reconstruct anything the structured summary left out of it.
The commitments already made to the customer, such as a promised delivery date or a waived fee.

explanation: The two reported failures are duplicated actions and contradicted promises, so the handoff has to state what was already done and what was already said.

why.A: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and says nothing about what has already happened.
why.C: A transcript makes the human hunt for the two facts that matter instead of handing them over.

stem: A customer writes: "the replacement arrived with the same crack, my invoice still shows the old address, and I was promised a call back on Tuesday that never came." Across 300 similar tickets, the agent answers the first concern well and never mentions the other two in 23% of them. What design change fits?

options.text: Instruct the agent to answer the most urgent concern first and invite the customer to open separate tickets for the rest.
Escalate any message containing more than one concern, since combined tickets are where the agent underperforms.
Run three independent agent sessions, one per concern, and send the customer each reply as it comes back.
Split the message into distinct items, investigate each against the same customer context, then reply once.

explanation: Multi-concern messages should be decomposed into distinct items, investigated against shared context, then synthesized into one unified resolution.

why.A: Moves work the agent should do onto the customer and pushes first-contact resolution down.
why.B: Multi-concern tickets are common, and escalating all of them abandons the resolution target.
why.C: Three isolated sessions cannot see each other's findings and send one customer three replies.

stem: Four rules currently live in your pipeline agent's system prompt. Compliance sampling over 5,000 runs puts each rule between 96% and 99%. Which two of them need programmatic enforcement rather than prompt guidance? (Select 2)

options.text: The merge tool may not be called until the security scan tool has returned a completed result.
The delete_branch tool may not be called unless the pull request status returned by the API is "merged".
Every review comment should name a concrete suggested fix rather than only describing the problem.
Related comments should be grouped into one thread so reviewers receive fewer separate notifications.

explanation: A few failures in a hundred are tolerable for comment style, but not for merging unscanned code or deleting an unmerged branch, where the consequence is irreversible.

why.C: Comment quality is a preference with no irreversible consequence, so prompt guidance is proportionate.
why.D: Notification grouping is a presentation choice, and an occasional miss costs nothing.

stem: Policy says your deployment agent may not call deploy_production for a change with no signed approval. The team implemented this as a PostToolUse hook on deploy_production that looks up the approval and appends "UNAPPROVED" to the tool result when none exists. The hook fired twice last quarter, the agent reported both correctly in its summary, and both unapproved changes were live for about 40 minutes. What is wrong with the design?

options.text: PostToolUse runs after the call has executed, so the block belongs in a PreToolUse hook on deploy_production.
The hook annotates the result instead of raising an error, so the agent treats the deploy as an ordinary success.
The approval rule belongs in the system prompt, where the agent can apply it before it decides to deploy at all.
The hook should trigger an automatic rollback when it finds no approval, so the exposure window closes without a human.

explanation: A PostToolUse hook sees the result of a call that already ran. Policy here forbids the call itself, so enforcement has to intercept the outgoing tool call and block it before it executes.

why.B: The agent did report both correctly. The message is not the problem; by the time the hook runs the deploy has happened.
why.C: A prompt rule has a non-zero failure rate, and the policy asks for a guarantee rather than a reduction.
why.D: A compensating action still lets unapproved code reach production, and not every deploy can be rolled back.

stem: Two MCP servers your agent uses return file modification times differently, one as epoch milliseconds and one as ISO 8601. You shipped a hook to normalize them, but the staleness comparison error rate is unchanged at 8%. The hook is registered as an interception that runs before each tool call and rewrites the call's arguments. What is wrong?

options.text: The hook is registered against only one of the two servers, so half the timestamps still arrive unconverted.
Interception hooks cannot modify data, so the conversion belongs in the tool descriptions instead.
The timestamps exist only in the returned result, so the conversion belongs in a PostToolUse hook.
The result payload is what the model reads, so the prompt should tell it to convert before comparing.

explanation: A hook that runs before the call can only see the arguments. The timestamps appear in the result, so normalization has to happen on the way back with PostToolUse.

why.A: Registering it against both servers changes nothing, because neither call carries a timestamp in its arguments.
why.B: Interception hooks do act on what they intercept; the issue is that the data does not exist yet at that point.
why.D: Puts deterministic conversion back into the model on every comparison, which is what the hook was meant to remove.

stem: Three MCP search servers return records in the same shape, with no field naming the server or the retrieval time. Spot checks show your reports attribute about 1 claim in 9 to the wrong source, and readers cannot tell which of two contradicting figures was retrieved more recently. What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Have the coordinator note in the synthesis prompt which of the three servers was called for each subtopic of the research.
A PostToolUse hook that stamps the source server and retrieval time onto each record before it enters context.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to track which tool returned each result as it reads through the findings.
Call one search server per run and merge the three runs afterwards, so each record's origin is unambiguous.

explanation: Attaching provenance to each record is deterministic, and a PostToolUse hook puts the source and time next to the data the model actually reads.

why.A: A subtopic-level note cannot say which of three servers returned any particular record.
why.C: Asks the model to maintain bookkeeping that the tool results could carry for free.
why.D: Restructures the pipeline and triples the runs to recover a field a hook can add.

stem: Your CI review first asks the model to plan the review for this pull request, then follows that plan. Across 60 runs the plans differ: error handling was examined in 38 of them, input validation in 21, and two runs reviewed only formatting. The pull requests are all routine feature work against the same service. What restructuring fits?

options.text: Keep the generated plan but require every plan to include the four review categories the team cares about.
Generate three plans per run and review with the union of them, so a category is unlikely to be dropped.
Score each generated plan against a rubric and regenerate it whenever the score falls below the threshold.
Replace the per-run plan with a fixed chain of focused passes applied to every pull request.

explanation: The work is the same on every pull request, so the decomposition should be fixed rather than re-invented per run. Dynamic decomposition earns its cost only when later subtasks depend on what earlier steps discover.

why.A: A generated plan required to always contain the same four items is a fixed chain with a probability attached.
why.B: Three plans cost three times as much and can still all skip the same category.
why.C: Adds scoring and regeneration machinery to force variation out of a step that never needed to vary.

stem: Your Claude Code migration runs one local pass per file to rewrite calls to the legacy client, then a cross-file pass to catch what those rewrites broke. The cross-file pass receives the full text of all 34 touched files, and its findings have turned generic. Last week it missed a rewritten helper whose return type changed, while three callers sitting in files that no local pass flagged still expect the old one. What should the cross-file pass receive instead?

options.text: The structured output of each local pass: the signatures that changed, what each file exports, and where it is called.
The 34 files split across three cross-file passes, with a fourth pass merging the findings those three produce.
The same 34 files, ordered so the most heavily changed ones sit at the start of the prompt where attention is strongest.
Only the files whose local pass reported a change, with their full text, so the pass reads less and stays specific.

explanation: The integration pass needs the contracts, not the source. Feeding it every file makes it re-derive at 34 file scale what each local pass already established, which is where the specificity goes.

why.B: Splitting the integration pass rebuilds the boundaries that pass exists to look across, so a caller can land in a different split than its helper.
why.C: Ordering does not reduce what the pass has to hold; it still reads 34 files to find one changed signature.
why.D: Drops the files no local pass flagged, which is exactly where the callers left on the old contract are sitting.

stem: Your team runs four recurring Claude Code jobs and wants each on the right decomposition strategy. Which two are best served by a fixed prompt chain rather than a plan generated per run? (Select 2)

options.text: The weekly triage of newly failing tests, where the cause differs each week and usually sits outside the failing file.
The quarterly investigation into why dev server boot time keeps growing, which starts from a symptom and no suspect.
The dependency bump review, which checks the changelog, the lockfile diff, the breaking-change notes and the test run.
The release-notes pass, which reads the merged pull requests, groups them by area and drafts one entry per group.

explanation: C and D apply the same known steps to different inputs every time, which is what prompt chaining is for. Both other jobs start from a symptom whose next step depends on what the previous step turned up.

why.A: A triage whose cause differs weekly needs subtasks generated from what each step discovers.
why.B: An open investigation with no suspect cannot be reduced to a fixed sequence written in advance.

stem: You have three long investigations open in the same repository and you resume each morning by picking up the most recent session. Twice last week you resumed into the wrong investigation and worked for about 20 minutes before noticing, because the agent answered confidently out of the context of a different investigation. What should you change?

options.text: Carry one investigation at a time to completion, so there is only ever one session to resume.
Start fresh each morning and re-explore, since three overlapping sessions cannot be told apart reliably.
Give each investigation a session name and resume it by that name rather than by recency.
Open each resumed session by asking the agent what it was working on, and switch sessions when the answer is wrong.

explanation: Named sessions make resumption a deliberate choice. Resuming by recency selects whichever session you touched last, which is not the same as the one you meant to continue.

why.A: Serializes three investigations to work around a selection problem that a session name solves.
why.B: Discards context that is still valid and pays for re-exploration every morning.
why.D: Detects the mistake after loading the wrong session instead of loading the right one, and costs a round trip each time.

stem: Your investigation session is three days old and the service was restructured underneath it, so you decide to start fresh rather than resume. You want the new session productive on the first prompt. What should the summary you inject contain?

options.text: The conclusions that still hold, written as statements, with the file paths and identifiers each one refers to.
The previous session's tool results, so the new session works from the same raw material the old one had.
The list of prompts you asked in the old session, so the new one follows the same line of investigation.
The old session's name and a note to resume it whenever the new session needs the earlier detail.

explanation: You start fresh precisely because the prior tool results are stale. What carries over is the conclusions that are still true, stated plainly against the paths they concern.

why.B: Those results are the stale material that made resumption unsafe in the first place.
why.C: Prompts record what you asked, not what was learned, so the new session re-derives everything.
why.D: Reaches back into the session you abandoned, which brings the stale observations with it.

stem: A teammate proposes that each CI review job resume the previous job's session with --resume so repository exploration is not repeated, saving roughly 90 seconds per job. Jobs run on different pull request branches, and each one checks out a different tree. How should you evaluate the proposal?

options.text: Adopt it, and have each job run /compact first so the previous branch's exploration does not fill the context.
Reject it: each job checks out a different branch, so the prior session's file reads describe another tree.
Adopt it for jobs on the same branch only, and fork the previous session for every job on a different branch.
Adopt it and tell the resumed session which files this pull request changed, so it re-reads only those.

explanation: Resumption suits a session whose prior context is mostly still valid. Across branches the earlier file reads describe a different tree, so each job should start fresh.

why.A: Compaction summarizes stale content; it does not make any of it current.
why.C: A fork inherits the same out-of-date baseline, so the cross-branch problem is unchanged.
why.D: That note covers this pull request's changes but not the previous branch's, which stay in the session as if current.
